edits.old: At a positive threshold and in dimension at least two, \cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation} allows a smooth semipositive maximizer that is strictly positive outside a proper analytic set $Z$. It gives the exact global equation, smoothness off $Z$, and uniqueness of all threshold subsolutions modulo constants. The uniqueness proof takes the maximum of two subsolutions and uses a Gauduchon integral to remove the resulting nonpositive divisorial difference. It requires no prescribed singularity type. The classes of the positive pole divisors are then linearly independent by \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-divisor-independence}. Moreover, \cref{prop:semipositive-dual-exponential-limit} proves whole-family normalized $L^1$ convergence of the exponential solutions, with a fixed lower barrier and $b\leq c_\lambda\leq b\mathrm{e}^{C\lambda}$. If the threshold solution also admits a genuine smaller-background envelope, \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-capacity-limit} strengthens this to capacity convergence. For $f\in L^p$, $p>1$, \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-lp-limit} gives a continuous threshold solution and whole-family uniform convergence. The branched projective example in \cref{ex:semipositive-projective-maximizer} has a smooth threshold solution but a nondifferentiable density root along $Z$. For general $L^1$ data, automatic genuineness of the smaller-background envelope and global regularity across $Z$ remain open here.
edits.new:
At a positive threshold and in dimension at least two, \cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation} allows a smooth semipositive maximizer that is strictly positive outside a proper analytic set $Z$. It gives the exact global equation, smoothness off $Z$, and uniqueness of all threshold subsolutions modulo constants. The uniqueness proof takes the maximum of two subsolutions and uses a Gauduchon integral to remove the resulting nonpositive divisorial difference. It requires no prescribed singularity type. The classes of the positive pole divisors are then linearly independent by \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-divisor-independence}.

\Cref{prop:semipositive-dual-exponential-limit} proves whole-family normalized $L^1$ convergence of the exponential solutions, with a fixed lower barrier and $b\leq c_\lambda\leq b\mathrm{e}^{C\lambda}$. If the threshold solution also admits a genuine smaller-background envelope, \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-capacity-limit} strengthens this to capacity convergence. For $f\in L^p$, $p>1$, \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-lp-limit} gives a continuous threshold solution and whole-family uniform convergence. The branched projective example in \cref{ex:semipositive-projective-maximizer} has a smooth threshold solution but a nondifferentiable density root along $Z$. For general $L^1$ data, automatic genuineness of the smaller-background envelope and global regularity across $Z$ remain open here.

edits.old: The action is free. Indeed, $e^t=e^{\mathrm i t}=1$ forces $t=0$. It is proper: if both $(z,w)$ and $t\cdot(z,w)$ range in compact subsets of $\widetilde X$, the norms of all four vector components are bounded above and away from zero. Writing $t=a+\mathrm i b$, the ratios of the norms bound $e^a$ and $e^{-b}$ above and away from zero. Thus $a$ and $b$ stay bounded, which proves properness. The free proper holomorphic action has local holomorphic slices and a Hausdorff complex quotient $X$ of dimension three.
edits.new: The action is free. Indeed, $\mathrm{e}^t=\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm i t}=1$ forces $t=0$. It is proper: if both $(z,w)$ and $t\cdot(z,w)$ range in compact subsets of $\widetilde X$, the norms of all four vector components are bounded above and away from zero. Writing $t=a+\mathrm i b$, the ratios of the norms bound $\mathrm{e}^a$ and $\mathrm{e}^{-b}$ above and away from zero. Thus $a$ and $b$ stay bounded, which proves properness. The free proper holomorphic action has local holomorphic slices and a Hausdorff complex quotient $X$ of dimension three.

edits.old: This places a necessary restriction on any geometric use of the equation. A construction that assigns a canonical potential to arbitrary nonnegative data must specify a selection procedure and prove that it is well defined. Existence in the ordinary minimal singularity type does not provide such a selection. The unique scalar, and the corresponding variational volume for strictly positive data, remain meaningful without uniqueness of every potential. On a compact Hermitian surface, \cref{uni-cor:dense-lowdim} proves uniqueness for $C^2$ potentials and continuous density positive on a dense set, with no differential condition on the metric. In dimension three, \cref{uni-thm:sobolev} instead uses a sign condition on $\ddc\omega$. The cofactor identity in \cref{eq:mixed-uniqueness-defect} and the signed quadratic-difference argument provide two distinct integration mechanisms.

edits.old: Let $X$ be connected, $\omega$ Hermitian and $f\geq0$ smooth. Suppose $\{f>0\}$ is connected and dense. Are two bounded normalized solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u)=cf\,\mathrm{d}V$, with the same $c>0$, necessarily equal? Separately, for densities allowing nonuniqueness, do normalized solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u_\lambda)=e^{\lambda u_\lambda}f\,\mathrm{d}V$ select a unique limit as $\lambda\downarrow0$?
edits.new: Let $X$ be connected, $\omega$ Hermitian and $f\geq0$ smooth. Suppose $\{f>0\}$ is connected and dense. Are two bounded normalized solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u)=cf\,\mathrm{d}V$, with the same $c>0$, necessarily equal? Separately, for densities allowing nonuniqueness, do the solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\omega(u_\lambda)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda}f\,\mathrm{d}V$ converge uniformly after subtracting their suprema, as $\lambda\downarrow0$?

edits.old: For $C^{1,1}$ potentials the first question is answered affirmatively by \cref{uni-thm:anchors}. The remaining issue is the passage to bounded potentials. All the hypersurface counterexamples here have three positive-density components; even the analytic density in \cref{uni-thm:analytic-example} has exactly this topology. The second asks for a canonical limit, and does not follow from uniqueness of the positive-exponent equation at each fixed parameter. A selection could exist even when the limiting equation has several solutions. These counterexamples do not refute \cref{conj:continuous-gaud-adjoint}: that conjecture uses a finite continuous logarithmic density $F$, for which $e^F$ is strictly positive. The logarithms of the degenerate densities have no finite continuous extensions across their zero sets.
